common_name: AC Greenfix Chickling Vetch (Drought-Tolerant Prairie Green Manure Grass Pea)

planting.note: Drill inoculated seed as early as the ground can be worked in spring, the same window used for field peas, since this chickling vetch establishes best in cool soil and tolerates a late spring frost.

directions: AC Greenfix was bred at the Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada research station in Swift Current from a mass selection of chickling vetch for biomass yield and smaller seed size, giving Canadian Prairie growers an annual legume green manure that tolerates dry conditions better than most cover crop legumes. Seed it with a standard pea or lentil inoculant at a rate similar to field peas, and expect a dense, weed-suppressing ground cover within about two months even on as little as eight inches of growing-season moisture. The sprawling, viney growth carries a mix of blue and pink flowers followed by darker, sometimes speckled seed pods. Terminate by tillage, roller-crimping, or herbicide before a following cash crop to release the fixed nitrogen.

planting.note: Seed in early spring, often underseeded with a small grain nurse crop, so the biennial taproot can establish through its first season before overwintering and regrowing the following spring.

directions: Polara was bred in Canada as a low-coumarin white sweetclover, greatly reducing the risk of dicoumarol poisoning in livestock that can occur when standard high-coumarin sweetclover hay spoils or molds. It matures earlier than older white sweetclover strains and tolerates very cold winters, making it a reliable biennial green manure and grazing legume across the northern Great Plains and Canadian Prairies. The deep taproot breaks up compacted subsoil and scavenges nutrients from well below the reach of most annual cover crops, while the extensive root system builds soil structure over its two-year cycle. Mow or incorporate in late spring of the second year, near early bloom, to maximize nitrogen contribution before seed set.

common_name: SoilSaver Black Oat (Cold-Tolerant Nematode-Suppressing Winter Cover Oat)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill in early to mid-fall in the lower Southeast; SoilSaver was selected jointly by Auburn University and Brazil's IAPAR specifically for improved cold tolerance over older black oat strains, though it still winter-kills reliably in colder zones.

directions: SoilSaver is the only black oat cultivar bred specifically for the southeastern United States, released jointly by Auburn University and USDA-ARS in cooperation with Brazil's Instituto Agronomico do Parana, where black oat has long been a staple no-till cover crop. It was selected for improved cold tolerance over older black oat lines and for suppressing root-lesion and stubby-root nematodes ahead of vegetable or row-crop plantings. The fine-textured, fast-growing canopy produces dry matter comparable to winter rye or wheat while carrying a higher nitrogen concentration and lower carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, so its residue breaks down faster than cereal rye mulch. Grow it alone for a quick-decomposing weed-suppressing mat, or mix it with a legume such as crimson clover or hairy vetch to add a nitrogen-fixing component to the stand.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service Plant Materials Program
